profile.a: The author, drawing on his time as Head of AI and Digital Transformation at one of the largest UK banks, writing for Organisational Behaviour and Leadership.
The C-suite and senior managers of a conventional retail bank trying to become AI-driven.
Why AI transformation in retail banks stalls on culture rather than technology, and a five-stage route to change it.
Handed in on 6 January 2025. Banks' generative AI spending is forecast to rise from $6bn in 2024 to $85bn in 2030.
UK retail banking, with comparisons to Deutsche Bank's Open Banking payments work in Poland and Commonwealth Bank of Australia's generative AI programme.
Challenger banks without branches threaten incumbents, but legacy hierarchy, a unionised workforce and fear of job losses after branch closures slow adoption even when budgets exist.

The three-level culture model (artifacts, espoused values, underlying assumptions) diagnoses the bank; the change framework (shared need, vision, commitment, monitoring, making change last) prescribes the route; OKRs measure progress.

charts.title: Banks' generative AI spending forecast ($bn)
charts.takeaway: Spending rises about 14 times in six years, roughly 56% a year. The paper's point is that money is no longer the constraint: the bank that fails will fail on culture.

charts.title: The bank's culture on three levels

items.title: Artifacts
items: Specialist AI teams
Code repositories
Regular risk and progress sessions
Dashboards on algorithm performance

items.title: Espoused values
items: Generic C-level AI strategy
Customer-satisfaction targets
FCA guidance on ethical AI
AI risk policies with vague value attribution

items.title: Underlying assumptions
items: A unionised workforce slows sudden change
Transformation seen as branding
AI means job losses after branch closures
Operations treats C-level views as aspirational

charts.takeaway: The gap sits between the levels: the bank has the artifacts and says the right things, but the assumptions underneath work against both. That is why a sound strategy can still stall.

charts.title: The change route the paper prescribes

items.title: Create a shared need
items.text: Present AI as creative destruction needed to survive challenger banks, not as a cost.

items.title: Shape a vision
items.text: Use Open Banking as the trigger for new services and a short transformative purpose such as 'the best customised digital journey'.

items.title: Mobilise commitment
items.text: Define the problem precisely, make goals public, tolerate failure but not incompetence, use political intelligence.

items.title: Monitor progress
items.text: OKRs: +10% revenue a year from AI, with key results on digital adoption and net promoter score.

items.title: Make change last
items.text: A central AI Council, training, flatter information flow, and a CEO success story.

charts.takeaway: Artifacts change first; assumptions change only with consistent behaviour over time, so the later stages carry the most weight.

charts.title: What resists the change and what the paper uses against it

left.title: Sources of resistance
items: Fear of redundancy and skill obsolescence
Silos between data scientists, IT and business units
Risk aversion driven by regulation
Leaders without a clear AI vision
Training and skill gaps

right.title: Levers proposed
items: Clear communication of how roles change
Central AI Council and cross-functional teams
Experimentation within compliance limits
Leadership alignment and a success narrative
Upskilling with realistic goals and tools

charts.takeaway: Each resistance point has a matching lever; the paper does not say which lever moved the assumptions in the author's own bank.
